_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: He shall vow benefit: he shall vow never to remarry her, for perhaps he divorces her as a ruse, so that she collects her marriage contract from the consecrated property, and then he remarries her.
tosafot:a1.1: When he divorces her he shall vow benefit: My teacher found this puzzling: why should he vow benefit? What is he doing? Surely he does not want her to collect from the consecrated property. On the contrary, they should have penalized the woman for collecting from the consecrated property! One can answer: since we are concerned that perhaps he made a collusion against the Temple, or against the guarantor whom he brought in to guarantee her, the Rabbis did not penalize her; and it is he who ought to vow, since [we cannot] know whether his intention is a ruse, and once they have made him vow, his intention will not help him.
gershom:a1.1: One who consecrates his property and there was the marriage contract of a woman upon him: the property was liened to the marriage contract, so the consecration is not a complete consecration, and if he divorces his wife she collects from that consecrated property.
gershom:a2.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: When he divorces her, he shall make her vow: he shall vow benefit, that he will not remarry her nor benefit from her again, since we are concerned that perhaps he did this by a ruse: that he divorces her for this purpose, so that she collects her marriage contract from the consecrated property, and afterward he will remarry her and they will consume the property together.
gershom:a3.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua says: He need not make her vow.
gershom:a4.1: The guarantor of a woman for her marriage contract: a man who became her guarantor on behalf of her husband at the time of her marriage, that if her husband does not pay her marriage contract when he divorces her, he will pay her; and her husband was divorcing her so that she would turn to the guarantor and claim her marriage contract from him.
gershom:a5.1: He shall make her vow: since we are concerned that perhaps they made a collusion.
rashi:a3.1: Let us say he stated his teaching according to [one side of] a dispute of tanna’im: and it is not the opinion of all.
tosafot:a3.1: In brief: Tosafot ask: in the last chapter of Bava Batra (175a) Rav Huna’s statement is set in a case where the creditor holds a document. Then how does a concern of collusion apply here, since the document is validated in that creditor’s hand and he is certainly telling the truth? They answer that there must still be a concern of collusion: had the dying man not said “So-and-so has one hundred in my possession,” the creditor, even holding a document, would collect only with an oath; now that he said it, the creditor collects without an oath. So too in chapter Shevuat HaDayanim (Shevuot 42b), on the mishna “one takes an oath for a minor and for the Temple”: the Gemara explains it as a creditor collecting from consecrated property, asks that it is no different from liened property of a commoner, answers that one might have thought a person colludes against a commoner but not against the Temple, and cites Rav Huna, concluding that this holds for one on his deathbed, since a person does not sin not for himself, but a healthy person does collude against the Temple. So there the collusion concerns the oath, and the same here. Tosafot then find it puzzling: by that conclusion a healthy person colludes against the Temple, yet here the Gemara says that for a healthy person Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one does not, so Rav Huna would be against Rabbi Yehoshua. They answer that a healthy person makes a minor collusion against the Temple, such as freeing [the creditor] from an oath; and still the Gemara rightly brings Rav Huna to bear on the mishna, all the more so: if Rav Huna says that a person does not collude against the Temple even over an oath, [all the more so the mishna’s collusion of divorcing his wife]. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a6.1: So-and-so has one hundred in my possession, he is deemed credible: for that hundred is not consecrated, since it is not his.
rashi:a4.1: Only with regard to a healthy person: for there Rabbi Eliezer says a person colludes against the Temple, since what he takes from the Temple will be his.
rashi:a4.2: But with regard to a person on his deathbed: who is about to die.
rashi:a4.3: A person does not sin when it is not for himself: he will not sin in order to profit someone else. [On the next explanation:] Rabbi Eliezer holds that since we make him vow in public that he will not remarry her, it no longer has nullification; therefore the vow is effective, and we make him vow.
tosafot:a4.1: For there is a presumption that a person does not sin when it is not for himself: that is why he is trusted to have [the creditor] collect without an oath, even though one does not attend to [collection from] liened property, or from consecrated property, which is like liened property, except with an oath, as is stated in chapter Shevuat HaDayanim (Shevuot 42b). And since we are not concerned that he colluded to admit how much he owes, so too there is no concern here that he divorces his wife in order to remarry her, as it is not reasonable that he would collude against the Temple through divorce any more than one on his deathbed [would through an admission].
gershom:a7.1: Everyone agrees: both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, that he is deemed credible.
gershom:a8.1: For a person who is dying does not sin by saying that it is not consecrated, for the sake of another, unless it is certainly so.
rashi:a5.1: It has nullification: and that is why he need not [vow], since it would accomplish nothing.
tosafot:a5.1: One Sage holds it has nullification: And if you say: even granting that it has nullification, we hold that one must specify the vow [before the Sage], so when he comes before a Sage, the Sage will not nullify it! One can answer that he need specify only the wording in which he vowed, not why he vowed. It is unlike the case in chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 35b) of a priest who married a woman in transgression, about which it says that he vows and divorces her, and where you say that he must specify, and therefore a Sage will not release him: there he vows not to benefit from his disqualified wife, and when he comes before a Sage and explains his vow, the Sage will not release him. But here [the Sage] will not refrain from releasing him even if he hears the wording of his vow.
gershom:a9.1: With regard to a vow administered in public: that he vowed concerning his wife in public; about this they disagree.
gershom:a11.1: It has nullification: so it accomplishes nothing. Therefore what benefit is there in making him vow concerning her? Once she has collected her marriage contract, he will have it nullified.
gershom:a12.1: And Rabbi Eliezer holds it has no nullification.
rashi:a6.1: On the consent of the public: who say to him: Vow.
gershom:a13.1: On the consent of the public: that the public obliged him to vow concerning her.
gershom:a14.1: And furthermore, that which is taught: Rabbi Yehoshua says: He need not make her vow.
gershom:a15.1: He should have said: It is ineffective for him to vow concerning her, since it has nullification.
rashi:a8.1: They disagree about requesting [dissolution] of consecration: Rabbi Eliezer holds that one may not request of a Sage [the dissolution of] consecration; even if he says to the Sage, I did not vow with this in mind, and it is a mistaken consecration, even so the Sage does not release his vow. Therefore this man who divorces his wife after consecrating regrets it, finds no Sage to release him, and so makes this collusion. And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one may request [dissolution] of consecration, and here he need not vow benefit: for if it were for collusion that he acted, he would request the dissolution of his vows and would not need to divorce her.
tosafot:a8.1: They disagree about requesting [dissolution] of consecration: that is, according to Rabbi Yehoshua there is a request, so he need not be made to vow benefit from his wife if he divorces her, since we are not concerned that he divorces her through collusion to collect from the consecrated property: why would he need to divorce her? He can request [dissolution] of the consecration, it will be a mistaken consecration, and then it will not be consecrated. And it is somewhat puzzling: we hold like Beit Hillel that mistaken consecration is not consecration, so there is a request; then how does Rav Huna say that a healthy person does collude against the Temple? Why should he collude, since he can request [dissolution] of his consecration, as Rabbi Yehoshua said? According to what I explained above it is well: a collusion over an oath, a light matter, he does, and does not request [dissolution] of his consecration; but something like divorcing his wife in order to remarry her he does not do, since he can request [dissolution] of his consecration.
gershom:a16.1: They disagree about requesting [dissolution] of consecration: when he consecrated his property, divorced his wife and she collected her marriage contract, what is [the law]? Can this consecrator request [dissolution] of his consecration before a Sage, saying: Had I known that she could come and collect her marriage contract from the consecrated property, I would not have consecrated, so that it turns out it was not consecration, since it was a mistaken consecration? And perhaps he will remarry his wife and they will consume the property. Therefore Rabbi Eliezer holds he must vow benefit concerning her, so that he will not request [dissolution]; and Rabbi Yehoshua holds he need not vow concerning her, since a person cannot request [dissolution] of consecration: even if he says, I did not consecrate with this in mind, it is still consecration, since mistaken consecration is consecration. [Rabbeinu Gershom thus pairs the two positions the other way around from Rashi and the Davidson English; see his note on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.]
rashi:a9.1: And it is taught: [stated] as support, that they disagree about requesting [dissolution].
gershom:a17.1: And it is taught: as support.
rashi:a9.2: This is the statement of Beit Shammai, this is the statement of Beit Hillel: the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is also the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
rashi:a10.1: Mistaken consecration is consecration: and there is no request [for dissolution] of consecration. A mistaken consecration is, for example, [one who says:] The white ox that comes out of my house first is consecrated, and a black one came out.
gershom:a18.1: Beit Shammai are like Rabbi Yehoshua, and one does not request [dissolution]; and Beit Hillel are like Rabbi Eliezer, and one does request; therefore he must make her vow. [A note printed with the commentary observes that this is the reverse of all the other commentators, for whom Rabbi Eliezer holds there is a request for consecration, like Beit Hillel, and suggests the Rambam (Hilkhot Arakhin 7) explained the same way. The baraita as printed pairs Rabbi Eliezer with Beit Shammai.]
gershom:a19.1: And he was hard-pressed: for he had come down from his wealth.
gershom:a20.1: But we learned: He shall vow benefit: for the court before which he divorces her will tell him: Vow benefit, that you will never remarry her.
rashi:a12.1: Is that to say that anyone who divorces, divorces in court: where they would tell him, Vow benefit? Let him go privately and divorce her.
gershom:a21.1: Is that to say that anyone who divorces divorces in court? He can divorce even before three laymen, who do not know that he must be made to vow. [A note printed with the commentary suggests the reading “in the great court,” as Rabbeinu Gershom reads explicitly in Bava Batra 174.]
rashi:a12.2: That he was a priest: Rav Huna; and had he divorced her he could not have remarried her.
gershom:a22.1: That he was a priest: who is forbidden to a divorcée.
rashi:a13.1: In accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: in tractate Ketubot (95b): One who says at the time of death, My property is yours and after you so-and-so’s, and the first went ahead and sold [and consumed etc.], Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The second has only what the first left over. And here too, [the one who gives such advice] is a wily, wicked person.
gershom:a23.1: One who advises to sell property etc.: My property is yours and after you so-and-so’s; the first went ahead, sold and consumed. The second takes it from the buyers; this is the statement of Rabbi. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The second has only what the first left over. Here too, it was wickedness and cunning that he gave him this advice.
gershom:a24.1: His son is different: since he reckons that in the end [his son] is fit to inherit from him.
gershom:a25.1: And a Torah scholar is different: for it is a mitzva to give him advice, so that he will have property and occupy himself with Torah.
tosafot:a15.1: And let him derive that he is a guarantor etc.: It is puzzling: why did [the Gemara] not raise this, of all these objections, against the mishna? One can answer that it did not want to raise it against the mishna, since the answer was simple: [the husband] had [property] and it was blighted.
gershom:a26.1: For the guarantor of a marriage contract is not bound, as is said below.
rashi:b1.1: He was a kablan: Rav Huna had given her movables as a pledge for her marriage contract, and she handed them over to his father; and that is a kablan, one who deals and gives by hand.
gershom:b1.1: He was a kablan: for example, her husband gave her a pledge for her marriage contract at the time of her marriage, and she gave it to her father-in-law, who trusted his son; and so he was bound. Alternatively, her father-in-law said to her: Give to your husband, and I am a kablan.
rashi:b1.2: If he does not have: if the borrower has no property at the time of the loan, the guarantor is not bound by his statement: since there is nothing to collect from the borrower, he does not resolve to bind himself.
gershom:b2.1: Even though the borrower has no property: at the time of the kablan’s undertaking, [the kablan] binds himself in his place; therefore she can collect the marriage contract from her father-in-law.
gershom:b3.1: What can be said: for it is assumed that Rav Huna had no property at the time [his] father became a kablan, and [the father] was not bound. And if you wish, say: a father, for his son, binds himself to be a kablan even though his son has no property.
rashi:b3.1: As it was stated: this refers back to what we said above: This works out well according to the one who says a kablan etc.
rashi:b3.2: The guarantor of a marriage contract, everyone agrees, is not bound: since he is performing a mitzva by matching them, and she lacks nothing, as she did not give money.
gershom:b4.1: A kablan for a creditor: who says to the lender: Give to him, and I am a kablan.
gershom:b5.1: Everyone agrees he is bound: for he becomes as if he had received the money from the lender’s hand.
rashi:b4.1: We read: “and she lacked nothing.” [Rashi’s text reads ḥasrah, “she lacked,” where the printed Aramaic reads ḥasreih.]
gershom:b6.1: He performs a mitzva: that he took it upon himself to marry them off, to match them; and she lacked nothing, since he received nothing from her hand; he merely said a word to her.
gershom:b7.1: A certain man who sold his property: without his wife’s knowledge.
gershom:b8.1: And he divorced his wife: and she wanted to collect her marriage contract from the buyers.
rashi:b5.1: We learned guarantor: that we are concerned that perhaps they will collude against him, and he vows benefit.
rashi:b5.2: What of a buyer: are we concerned for collusion, that after she seizes this land from the buyer he will remarry her, so that he must vow benefit?
tosafot:b5.1: We learned guarantor, we learned consecrated property; what of a buyer: My teacher found this puzzling: did he not know that throughout the Talmud a woman collects her marriage contract from buyers? And as for the Sages of Neharde’a, who also say she does not collect, why would she not collect from the buyers? Perhaps one can say that he sold his property and divorced her immediately, and that is why there was a concern of collusion; but had the sale been long before the divorce, and he divorced her later, we would not be concerned about collusion.
gershom:b9.1: We learned guarantor, we learned one who divorces, we learned consecrated property: that he must vow benefit concerning her, since we are concerned that perhaps they made a collusion.
gershom:b10.1: What of a buyer: must the seller who divorces vow benefit concerning her, since we are concerned that perhaps they made a collusion against the buyers?
rashi:b5.3: Like a peddler, reckoning and going on: like a merchant who counts his coins. That is, he taught these, and the same is true of a buyer.
gershom:b11.1: The tanna, like a peddler etc.: that is, the same is true of a buyer.
gershom:b12.1: What we did not learn we did not learn: a buyer, about whom we did not learn that he must make her vow, he does not make her vow.
gershom:b13.1: Due to the profit of the Temple: they attend to making him vow.
gershom:b14.1: A guarantor as well, since he performed a mitzva: in matching them; for this reason they attend to making him vow, so that a person will not refrain from performing a mitzva.
rashi:b7.1: Why should he go and purchase: as a rhetorical question: did he have to buy?
gershom:b15.1: For each and every one who is married knows that his property is liened to his wife’s marriage contract. Why did this buyer buy without the wife’s knowledge? Therefore they do not attend to making him vow.
rashi:b8.1: And there was the marriage contract of a woman upon him: where the divorce preceded the consecration, so there is no collusion.
gershom:b16.1: The woman cannot collect her marriage contract from the Temple: directly, since consecrated property does not go out without redemption; and also the consecration does not take effect on [the property], since a person cannot consecrate what is not his.
rashi:b8.2: Rather, the one who redeems redeems: the owners redeem it from the Temple cheaply, for a dinar or some small thing, in order to pay, for certainly the consecration does not take effect on it, since it is not his. And this small thing is due to a decree, as the Gemara explains.
tosafot:b8.1: The one who redeems redeems: by Rashi’s explanation this would be the same case explained afterward: he consecrated ninety and his debt was a hundred, he adds another dinar. But the wording does not imply so. Therefore it seems one should explain that here it deals with a case where the debt does not equal the property, for example he consecrated a hundred and his debt was ninety maneh. And this is the meaning: the one who redeems, that is, whoever wishes to redeem, may redeem from the Temple and pay the value of the surplus, since the property exceeds the debt; and all the property goes out to non-sacred status through this, since the consecration did not take effect on the part corresponding to the debt, and it looks as if he redeemed it all, so we do not say that consecrated property goes out without redemption. And the redeemer gives the woman her marriage contract or the creditor [his debt].
rashi:b8.3: He adds another dinar: the creditor lends this man another dinar, and he redeems this property.
tosafot:b8.2: He adds another dinar etc.: Rashi explained: the creditor will lend him another dinar and he redeems this property. By his explanation it implies that the creditor himself redeems, but the wording of the mishna does not imply so, since it teaches “in order to give etc.” Therefore it seems one should explain that the borrower takes a further loan of a dinar and redeems this property in order to give the woman her marriage contract and the creditor his debt.
gershom:b17.1: Rather, the one who redeems redeems etc.: that is, whoever wishes to redeem this property may redeem it for a small thing, in order to give the woman her marriage contract etc. And how does he redeem for a small thing? He consecrated ninety maneh and his debt was a hundred maneh: the creditor adds another dinar and redeems the consecrated property with that dinar, in order etc.; even though one could say that since [the dinar] does not correspond to his debt, [the property] should not go out to non-sacred status.
rashi:b9.1: Why do I need to state the one who redeems redeems: let the woman and the creditor take it without redemption, since the consecration did not take effect on it, and a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.
rashi:b9.2: Rabbi Abbahu’s: in the last chapter (below, Arakhin 33a).
tosafot:b9.1: In brief: From here Rashi brings proof that Rava’s statement (Ketubot 59b), “consecration removes a lien,” applies only to consecration of the body itself, which is stringent, but not to consecration for monetary value: for here, by law, the consecration does not take effect on the property, since it is liened, and it needs redemption only because of Rabbi Abbahu’s “so that people will not say…” My teacher was in doubt about a borrower who has only movables, which are consecration of value, and consecrated them: does the consecration take effect or not? Certainly if he sold them the sale is valid and the creditor does not seize them from the buyer, since the creditor’s lien is not on movables; but with consecration it is uncertain. And one cannot prove [that consecration of value does not take effect even on movables] from Rashi’s explanation of Rava’s statement (Bava Kamma 33b), “One who made his ox a designated security and consecrated it, the creditor does not collect from it,” since that case can be set where he transferred movables to the creditor along with land, in which case the creditor’s lien does take effect on the movables, as is stated in chapter Ḥezkat HaBatim (Bava Batra 44b), and he would collect even from a buyer. And it seems that the mishna deals with all property, both land and movables, and says that the consecration does not take effect, and they need redemption only because of Rabbi Abbahu. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b10.1: If his debt corresponds to his consecrated property, he redeems: for a small thing, as we said. In such a case one can say that when he originally lent to him, he lent with the intent to collect from this property. But if not, if his debt was more than his consecrated property, he did not lend with this in mind but simply trusted him; therefore he does not collect from the consecrated property. Another version: And if not, he does not redeem, but takes it without redemption. The first I heard [from my teachers], and it is the main one.
tosafot:b11.1: And if not, he does not redeem: Rashi explained: and if not, if his debt is more than his consecrated property, he did not lend to him with this in mind; therefore he does not collect from the consecrated property. Another version: and if not, he does not redeem, but takes it without redemption; the first I heard, and it is the main one. End of his words. But the Tosefta of our tractate implies like the latter version, as it teaches explicitly: And if not, his consecration is nothing.
gershom:b18.1: And if his debt did not correspond to his consecrated property, that his debt was more, he does not redeem: since he must wait [for] that surplus, as there is nowhere to collect it from, so too let him wait for the whole debt until the borrower has other property, and he collects nothing from the consecrated property.
rashi:b11.1: And the Rabbis, up to what amount: they hold that he lent with this property in mind.
gershom:b19.1: And the Rabbis: of the mishna.
gershom:b20.1: Up to what amount: that is, how much less than his debt may the consecrated property be, so that the creditor may add a dinar and take it?
rashi:b11.2: Up to half: but less than half, no.
tosafot:b11.2: Up to half: this can be reconciled with both versions [of Rashi]: since it is worth less than half, certainly he did not lend with this in mind; and according to the latter version, since the debt is more than [double], the consecration does not take effect on it, and there is no concern that people will say consecrated property goes out without redemption.
gershom:b21.1: Up to half: until the consecrated property equals even half his debt. But if it is less than half his debt, since he must wait for most of his debt, let him wait for the whole debt until the borrower has [property], and leave the Temple what is its own.
rashi:b12.1: They repossess from them: the treasurer enters their houses and takes against their will. Food, clothing, a bed and phylacteries: for all of them we leave him money to buy them if he does not have them.
gershom:b22.1: To him they give clothing and food, but not to his wife or to his children.
rashi:b13.1: Of each and every type: for there is a craft that needs four or five tools.
rashi:b13.2: Matzadin: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). Megera [saw]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss); a knife full of notches that cuts quickly, like the kind comb-makers have.
gershom:b23.1: Ma’atzarin [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads with a resh]: (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b13.3: His pair: a pair of cattle are the tools of his craft.
gershom:b24.1: His pair: a pair of oxen.
rashi:b14.1: One type many and one type few: for example three adzes and one saw: he gives [him] two of the many, and the third goes to the treasurer.
rashi:b14.2: And whatever he has of the few: as much as he has, and we do not buy him another; just as until now this sufficed for him, so let it suffice for him now.
gershom:b25.1: If he had one type many: for example he had many adzes, and of one type few, for example he has only one saw: one does not say that he should sell of the adzes, of which he has many, and buy of the few, so that he would have two saws.
gershom:b26.1: And whatever he has of the few: that is, they do not add to the few, but give him that itself and no more, since until now he had only one.
rashi:b14.3: One who consecrates his property: the phylacteries are included in his property.
rashi:b14.4: They take up his phylacteries: and he redeems them.
gershom:b27.1: They take up his phylacteries: they take his phylacteries from him, since they too are called property.
